client_need: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
stem: A hospital unit uses one blood glucose meter for several clients. Which practice best follows current CDC infection-control guidance?

options.A: Use a meter designed for professional multi-patient use and clean and disinfect it after every client according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
options.B: Wipe the meter once at the end of the shift because a new lancet is used for each client.
options.C: Share any over-the-counter home glucose meter as long as visible blood is wiped away between clients.
options.D: Continue sharing the meter even if the manufacturer provides no validated cleaning and disinfection instructions.

rationale: A is correct. CDC recommends assigning blood glucose meters to individual patients whenever possible. If a meter must be shared in a health care or congregate setting, it should be a device designed for professional use and must be cleaned and disinfected after every use according to the manufacturer’s instructions. If the manufacturer does not specify how the device should be cleaned and disinfected, the meter should not be shared. B is insufficient because contamination can occur with each use. C is incorrect because over-the-counter home meters are not automatically suitable for professional multi-patient use. D directly contradicts CDC guidance.
educational_objective: When a blood glucose meter must be shared, use a device intended for professional multi-patient use and clean and disinfect it after every client according to manufacturer instructions; do not share a meter lacking validated reprocessing instructions.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
source_document_title: Considerations for Blood Glucose Monitoring and Insulin Administration
source_version_date: CDC page dated August 7, 2024; current as accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Blood glucose meters — whenever possible assign a meter to one person; if sharing is necessary, select a device designed for professional use and clean and disinfect after every use per manufacturer instructions; if the manufacturer does not specify cleaning/disinfection, do not share the meter
source_claim_supported: Shared glucose meters require validated cleaning and disinfection after every patient use and should be designed for professional multi-patient use; meters without manufacturer reprocessing instructions should not be shared.

correction_summary: Strengthened the source item by adding two CDC nuances missing from the original: a shared meter should be designed for professional multi-patient use, and it should not be shared if the manufacturer provides no cleaning/disinfection instructions. The after-every-client cleaning requirement was preserved.

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against current CDC injection-safety guidance for assisted blood glucose monitoring.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A reproduces the professional-use plus after-every-use reprocessing requirements. The final item avoids inventing a disinfectant product or contact time because those are manufacturer-specific.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; once-per-shift cleaning is inadequate for a shared meter.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; home-use meters are not automatically appropriate for multi-patient professional use.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; absence of manufacturer cleaning/disinfection instructions means the meter should not be shared.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A satisfies all CDC conditions for safe shared-meter use.
audit_findings.cueing: All four choices are realistic equipment-management practices.
audit_findings.blueprint: Directly aligned with infection prevention and equipment safety.
